title: Maximum of Minimum Values in All Subarrays
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` of length `n`. Answer one question for every window size `k` from `1` to `n`: among all contiguous subarrays of `nums` with exactly `k` elements, take the minimum of each one, and report the largest of those minimums.

Return an array `ans` of length `n` where `ans[i]` is the answer for window size `i + 1`.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every subarray and its minimum takes O(n²). Turn the question around: instead of asking "what is the best minimum for length `k`?", ask "for which lengths can `nums[i]` be the minimum?" `nums[i]` is the minimum of every window that stays between the nearest smaller value on its left and the nearest smaller value on its right. If that stretch has `width` elements, `nums[i]` is a candidate answer for every length up to `width`.

A monotonic stack finds both boundaries for all indices in one pass. Then record `nums[i]` only at length `width`, and let a backward pass carry each value down to shorter lengths: a window that fits in `width` cells also fits in fewer.

## Approach

1. Keep a stack of indices with increasing values. For each `i`, pop every index whose value is `>= nums[i]`; `i` is the right boundary of each popped index.
2. Whatever remains on top is the nearest strictly smaller value on the left: store it in `left[i]`, then push `i`.
3. For each index, `width = right[i] - left[i] - 1`; update `ans[width - 1]` with `nums[i]`.
4. Sweep `k` from `n - 2` down to `0`, setting `ans[k] = max(ans[k], ans[k + 1])`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [0, 1, 2, 4]` is increasing, so nothing is ever popped and `right` stays `[4, 4, 4, 4]`, while `left = [-1, 0, 1, 2]`. The widths are `4, 3, 2, 1`, so `ans[3] = 0`, `ans[2] = 1`, `ans[1] = 2`, `ans[0] = 4`. The backward sweep changes nothing, giving `[4, 2, 1, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index is pushed and popped at most once, plus two linear passes.
- Space: O(n): the boundary arrays, the stack and the answer.

## Pitfalls

- Without the backward sweep, lengths no value fills exactly stay at `0`; the answer for length `k` is never smaller than for `k + 1`.
- With equal values, popping on `>=` makes one copy (the last of a run) get the full width; the other copies get shorter widths, which is harmless.
- Fill `left` with `-1` and `right` with `n` so values without a smaller neighbour reach the array ends.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left[i]` | index of the nearest strictly smaller value to the left, or `-1` |
| `right[i]` | index of the first value `<= nums[i]` to the right, or `n` |
| `stack` | indices whose values increase from bottom to top |
| `width` | length of the longest window where `nums[i]` is the minimum |
| `ans[k]` | best minimum for windows of length `k + 1` |
